articles.title: The Wait That Grows Wings
articles.dek: For seventeen years it lives in total darkness with nothing to show for it. Then one night, it becomes something almost unrecognizable — and Paul says our waiting works the same way.
articles.quote: The wait was never empty. It was the making of the wings.
articles.body:
Somewhere in the soil of the eastern United States right now, a small brown insect is doing nothing that looks like progress. It has no wings. It cannot sing. It has not seen daylight in years. It is simply attached to a tree root, feeding, in the dark, waiting. This is the periodical cicada, and depending on its brood, it will do this for thirteen or seventeen years straight — longer than almost any other insect on earth lives at all.

Scientists have tracked these broods for over a century, and the wait itself is the strange part. The nymph doesn't sleep through it. It grows, molts underground five separate times, and somehow keeps count of the years passing above a ceiling of dirt it has never seen. Then, on a specific warm night — the same night, for millions of them across hundreds of miles, as if someone rang a bell only they can hear — they climb. They break the surface, find the nearest vertical surface, and split their own skin down the back. What crawls out is not a repaired version of the old body. It is a new one: pale, soft, folded wings compressed like origami against its back. Over the next hour, in the open air for the first time in its life, the wings pump full of fluid and unfurl. By morning, the ground is littered with empty brown shells, and the air is filled with something that can fly and sing, having spent nearly two decades as something that could do neither.

Paul is writing to a church that knows what it means to live underground. Believers in Rome are facing suspicion, hardship, the daily grind of a faith that costs something and shows little on the surface. And into that reality, in Romans 8, Paul doesn't offer them an escape from the waiting. He gives them a new way to understand it.

He starts with a claim so bold it almost sounds careless: "I consider that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18). Not eventually erased. Not eventually explained. Not worth comparing — as if he set the hardest thing in his life on one side of a scale and the glory to come on the other, and the needle didn't even move.

Then he does something remarkable. He doesn't stop at human suffering. He zooms out to include everything alive: "For the creation waits in eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed" (Rom 8:19). The Greek word behind "eager expectation" pictures someone craning their neck forward, straining to see around a corner. Paul says the whole created world — trees, rivers, soil, cicadas and all — is doing that. Straining forward. Not stuck. Not wasted. Waiting on purpose, toward something.

And then the verse that reframes the whole passage: "We know that the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to the present time" (Rom 8:22). Notice the image Paul reaches for. Not a prison sentence. Not a punishment being endured. Labor. The kind of pain that is doing something the whole time it hurts — a pain with a person on the other side of it.

I consider that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us.

Here is the turn worth sitting with: the cicada underground is not paused. It is not marking time until the real living starts. Entomologists have found that even in its earliest instar stages, the nymph is already forming the folded wing pads it won't use for over a decade — building, cell by cell, the exact thing it will need on the one night it finally needs it. The waiting and the making are the same process, just hidden from view.

That is what Paul means when he writes that "we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption to sonship" (Rom 8:23), and that "the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans" (Rom 8:26). You may feel like nothing is happening in your longest season — the diagnosis that hasn't resolved, the prayer that hasn't landed, the years that have simply had to be lived through one ordinary day at a time. Paul's picture says otherwise. Something is being formed in the dark that you will not fully see until the day you finally step into the light and it's already there, ready to unfold.

This is also why Romans 8:28 is so often misquoted and so rarely understood the way Paul meant it. He does not say all things are good. Underground years are not good. Depth charges of grief, the slow ache of unanswered longing — Paul does not soften any of it. He says "in all things God works for the good of those who love him" (Rom 8:28). The dark is not denied. It is being worked, the way a root system works soil no one can see, into something that will one day break the surface.

Paul lands the whole passage — arguably the most soaring paragraph he ever wrote — with a list almost breathless in its completeness: "neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom 8:38–39). Notice what is missing from that list: waiting. He names death, demons, height, depth, every power in heaven and on earth — and none of it, including the length and the darkness of your longest season, can put you outside the reach of that love. The years underground were never a sign you'd been forgotten. They were the years the love was doing its quietest, most necessary work.

So if you're in a season that feels like nothing but soil and silence — a marriage still healing, a body still recovering, a calling still unclear — let Paul's picture do something for you today. You are not stalled. You are not forgotten. Somewhere beneath what you can see, wings are already being folded into shape, cell by patient cell, for the day they'll finally be needed. The wait was never empty. It was the making of the wings.

articles.title: The Audit That Built the Temple
articles.dek: When officials showed up demanding to see the paperwork, no one expected the search for proof to end with more provision than the builders had ever had before.
articles.quote: You don't have to win the argument for God's work — you only have to keep pointing back to what he's already written down.
articles.body:
In the early 1980s, the Statue of Liberty was rusting from the inside out. Her copper skin had turned green a century earlier, but the real damage was hidden: the iron skeleton holding her up, designed by the same engineer who later built the Eiffel Tower, was corroding where it met the copper. Before anyone could fix her, they had to know exactly how she'd been built in the first place. So restorers didn't guess. They tracked down Gustave Eiffel's original 1880s blueprints, filed away for a hundred years in French archives, and checked every rivet and rib against the actual design. Only once the original plans were verified did Lee Iacocca, the Chrysler chairman tapped to lead the restoration effort, launch a public campaign that raised hundreds of millions of dollars — not from government coffers, but from ordinary people and companies who wanted to be part of it. The search for proof came first. The provision followed.

That order — proof first, provision after — is exactly what happens in Ezra 5 and 6, in a story with far more tension than most people realize when they skim past it.

The Jewish exiles had come home to Jerusalem and started rebuilding God's temple, encouraged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. But rebuilding always draws attention, and soon Tattenai, the Persian governor of the whole region west of the Euphrates, showed up with a blunt question: "Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and to finish it?" (Ezra 5:3). This wasn't idle curiosity. Questioning a building project in the Persian Empire could get it shut down permanently.

Here's what's easy to miss: the Jewish elders didn't get defensive. They didn't argue or posture. They simply told the truth, the whole sweep of it — how their ancestors had angered God and lost the first temple to Babylon, and how King Cyrus of Persia himself had later decreed that this very temple be rebuilt, even paying for it out of the royal treasury and returning the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken (Ezra 5:11–16). Then Tattenai did something remarkable. Instead of shutting the work down on his own authority, he wrote to King Darius and asked him to search the royal records himself to see if Cyrus's decree was real (Ezra 5:17).

Picture the wait that followed. The builders down tools. A letter traveling hundreds of miles to the capital. Everything now resting on whether a decree issued by a king who was long dead could still be found somewhere in the filing system of an empire that had swallowed up dozens of kingdoms and countless decrees. It would have been easy for that scroll to be lost, misfiled, or simply never found.

It wasn't. "King Darius issued an order, and they searched in the archives stored in the treasury at Babylon. A scroll was found in the citadel of Ecbatana in the province of Media, which had this memorandum written on it" (Ezra 6:1–2) — and there it was, Cyrus's original decree, word for word, confirming everything the elders had said.

But Darius didn't stop at confirming the truth. He escalated it. He wrote back not just to clear the Jews, but to fund them beyond anything they'd had before.

"Do not interfere with the work on this temple of God... I decree that you are to help these elders of the Jews in the construction of this house of God: Their expenses are to be fully paid out of the royal treasury, from the revenues of Trans-Euphrates, so that the work will not stop" (Ezra 6:7–8).

Read that again slowly. An investigation that began as a threat to shut the temple down ended with the Persian government paying its bills. Darius went further still — ordering that whatever the priests needed for daily offerings be supplied without fail, and asking only that they pray for him and his sons in return (Ezra 6:9–10). He even decreed that anyone who defied this order would be severely punished (Ezra 6:11–12). The audit meant to stop the work became the reason it never lacked again.

It's worth asking why it played out this way. Notice what the elders didn't do. They didn't out-argue Tattenai. They didn't lobby, negotiate, or spin the story to sound more impressive. They just told the truth plainly and let it be checked. The strength of their case wasn't in how persuasively they presented it — it was in the fact that it was true, and true things hold up under scrutiny, even scrutiny from a foreign king with no reason to care about their God.

That's the fresh angle worth sitting with here. We tend to treat being questioned — about our motives, our calling, our work, our integrity — as an attack to be repelled. Ezra 5 and 6 suggest a quieter way through: stay honest, keep pointing back to what's already true and already established, and let the record be the thing that defends you. You don't have to win the argument for God's work — you only have to keep pointing back to what he's already written down. The truth doesn't need you to fight for it nearly as often as it needs you to simply trust it.

This shows up in ordinary life more than we notice. A worker gets questioned about a decision that was actually approved months ago, and the temptation is to get loud rather than to calmly produce the email. A ministry gets challenged on why it does what it does, and the healthiest response isn't a defensive speech — it's a clear, honest account of how it started and who called it into being. Scrutiny, handled with a straight back and an open hand, has a way of turning into confirmation. And confirmation, as Darius proved, sometimes comes with resources you never had before.

The temple was finished not long after (Ezra 6:14–15), and the people celebrated its dedication with joy, then kept the Passover together — Jewish returnees and others who'd joined them, celebrating because "the Lord had filled them with joy" (Ezra 6:22). A building project that started as a target for suspicion ended as a reason for a whole community's celebration.

So if something you're building — a family, a small business, a ministry, a piece of your own integrity — is being questioned right now, take heart from Ecbatana. You don't need a better argument. You need a true story and a willingness to let it be checked. Keep a record, even a simple one in your own memory, of what God has already done and already promised in your life. When the questions come, you won't need to raise your voice. You'll just need to point, calmly, to what's already written down — and let him do the rest.

articles.title: Home Again, But Not Yet Alive
articles.dek: The skies cleared over the Philippines this week after Typhoon Kiyapo moved out — but Psalm 85 knows that a calm sky and a revived heart are two different gifts.
articles.quote: Being brought back is not the same as being brought alive — that's why we keep praying, even after the storm has passed.
articles.illustration: PAGASA clear skies after Typhoon Kiyapo
articles.body:
This week, PAGASA gave the country a small, ordinary miracle: four days with no tropical cyclone in sight. Typhoon Kiyapo had moved out, and behind it came something Filipinos know how to treasure — dry pavement, open skies, laundry finally strung across the line without a worried glance upward. In coastal towns, fishermen pushed their bancas back into water that had gone calm again. In the provinces, farmers walked out to check what was left standing in the rice fields. Sari-sari stores rolled up their shutters. Mothers swept the mud off their doorsteps and let the sun do the rest.

There is a particular kind of relief in a cleared sky after a storm — not just that the danger has passed, but that ordinary life can resume. You can hang out the wash. You can walk to the market without an umbrella. The land, so to speak, has been given back to you.

Psalm 85 opens on exactly that kind of relief. Most scholars place it after the Israelites returned from exile in Babylon — decades of displacement, finally over. The people are home. The land is theirs again. And the psalm begins by looking back at what God has already done: "You showed favor to your land, LORD; you restored the fortunes of Jacob. You forgave the iniquity of your people and covered all their sins. You set aside all your wrath and turned from your fierce anger" (Psalm 85:1–3). Three sentences, three plain facts. The storm is over. The exile has ended. God's anger has lifted like weather clearing.

And then, without warning, the psalm changes its tense. The same voice that just finished thanking God for a restoration already accomplished turns around and pleads for one all over again: "Restore us again, God our Savior, and put away your displeasure toward us. Will you be angry with us forever? Will you prolong your anger through all generations?" (Psalm 85:4–5).

Read it once and it looks like a contradiction. God already restored them — verse 1 says so plainly. Why is verse 4 begging for restoration as if it never happened?

Here is the thing worth noticing: the people were back in the land, but they were not yet alive in it. The exile had ended on paper, in geography, in the simple fact of standing on native soil again. But something in them was still bowed down, still waiting, still asking whether joy would ever really come home too. Being brought back to a place is not the same as being brought back to life. You can stand in the right country, in the right house, in the right season of blessing, and still feel the ache of a heart that hasn't caught up yet.

That is what makes the psalm's central question so tender:

"Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?" (Psalm 85:6)

The Hebrew word behind revive is the same word used for breathing life into something, for making dead bones live. It is not a request to fix circumstances — the circumstances, in this case, were already fixed. The exile was over. The land was theirs. What the psalmist is asking for is different: life, in the deepest sense of the word. Not just to be somewhere good again, but to feel it. Not just to be forgiven, but to feel forgiven enough to rejoice.

This is a mercy hiding inside an odd little psalm, and it is worth sitting with. Maybe your storm has technically passed. Maybe the diagnosis came back better than expected, the money finally arrived, the relationship mended, the exile — whatever shape it took for you — genuinely ended. And yet something in you still feels like it's standing in the wreckage, waiting for the feeling of being alive to match the fact of being safe. If that's you, you are not failing at gratitude. You are simply living in the gap the psalmist lived in — restored, but not yet revived. And the psalm gives you permission to name that gap out loud, to God, without shame.

Notice, too, that the psalmist doesn't try to manufacture the feeling. He doesn't grit his teeth and decide to rejoice by force of will. He asks God to do the reviving. "Show us your unfailing love, LORD, and grant us your salvation" (Psalm 85:7). The joy he's after isn't something he can talk himself into. It has to be given, the way sunlight is given to a field after weeks of rain — not manufactured, just received, in its own time.

There's a homely picture in that returned calm this week — boats back on quiet water, wash drying in a clean wind, farmers walking fields that are theirs again. It's a good picture of what God has already done for anyone who has been forgiven and brought home. But don't stop at the picture. If today you're standing in circumstances that have genuinely improved, and your heart still hasn't quite believed the good news yet, let Psalm 85:6 be your prayer exactly as it is: Will you not revive us again, that we may rejoice in you? Not a demand. Not a failure to be grateful. Just an honest, well-worn plea from people who know the difference between being brought back and being brought alive — and who trust the God who has already proven, once, that he's willing to do both.

So today, if the sky over your life has cleared but your heart hasn't quite stepped outside yet, say the words anyway. Ask to be revived, not just restored. Then wait for the feeling the way farmers wait for the sun — certain it's coming, even before it warms your face.

articles.title: Go Now, Sleep Later
articles.dek: A Harvard scientist discovered why a trapped animal never eases into its escape — Proverbs gives the same urgent command to anyone caught by their own words.
articles.quote: You don't have to thrash alone in that snare. Somebody already went in, at the point of exhaustion, and did not stop until you were free.
articles.body:
In 1915, a Harvard physiologist named Walter Cannon strapped instruments to frightened cats and watched something remarkable happen inside their bodies. The moment a cat sensed a dog nearby, its adrenal glands dumped a flood of adrenaline into its bloodstream almost instantly. Blood rushed away from digestion and toward the big muscles. Pupils widened. Blood sugar spiked for quick energy. Nothing about the response was gradual. The cat's whole body committed everything, all at once, to one purpose: get away, now. Cannon gave the discovery a name that's become common language: fight or flight. But the detail people miss is the timing. The body doesn't ease into an escape. It doesn't wait for a better moment. Once it's clear you're trapped, every system snaps to full alert in a heartbeat, because hesitation is the one thing a trapped creature cannot afford.

Proverbs 6 opens with a very different kind of trap, but the same urgent instinct. “My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, if you have shaken hands in pledge for a stranger... you have been trapped by what you said, ensnared by the words of your mouth” (Proverbs 6:1-2, NIV). In the ancient Near East, a handshake like this was a real legal contract. If your neighbor guaranteed a loan, agreed to cover someone else's debt if they defaulted, and shook hands on it, he was now legally on the hook for money he never borrowed. If the debtor vanished or came up short, the guarantor lost his land, his flocks, sometimes his freedom. It was an act of generosity that could quietly become a life sentence.

So picture this young man. Maybe a friend needed a loan and asked him to co-sign. Maybe it felt small in the moment, a way to help, a way to look generous in front of the town elders at the gate. He shook the hand. He walked home. And somewhere between the handshake and the harvest, the numbers turned against him. Now his own household is exposed for a debt that was never his idea. He didn't break a law. He kept his word. And that word is exactly what has him cornered. What does wisdom tell him to do? Not to feel bad about it. Not to wait and see if it resolves itself.

“Then do this, my son, to free yourself, since you have fallen into your neighbor's hands: Go — to the point of exhaustion — and give your neighbor no rest! Allow no sleep to your eyes, no slumber to your eyelids.” (Proverbs 6:3-4, NIV)

That is not gentle advice. That's a command to move like the cat in Cannon's lab: fully, immediately, without the comfortable delay of tomorrow. Verse 5 finishes the picture with two images every original reader would have instantly recognized: “Free yourself, like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the snare of the fowler” (Proverbs 6:5, NIV). A gazelle already gripped by a hunter doesn't politely negotiate its release. It thrashes with everything it has, because a half-effort changes nothing. Wisdom here isn't shaming the son for the mess he's in. It's telling him the truth about entrapment: you don't ease your way out of a snare. You go hard, right now, or you don't go at all.

Here's the detail worth sitting with, though. Notice that the whole warning in verse 1 begins with an if. The wisest move was never to be in this position in the first place — to count the cost before the handshake, not after (a caution Jesus later gives the crowds in Luke 14:28, about a builder who should sit down and estimate the price before laying the first stone). But Proverbs doesn't only speak to the cautious. It speaks to the son who already said yes, who already shook the hand, who is already caught. And to him, wisdom offers no shame spiral, no lecture about how he got here. Just urgency, and a way out.

That's worth noticing, because most of us are not reading this as hypothetical financial advice. We are reading it as people who have, at some point, been trapped by our own words — a promise made too quickly, a commitment that outgrew our ability to keep it, a yes we wish had been a no. And under all of it sits a deeper snare none of us signed up for and all of us are born into: a debt of our own we could never repay no matter how hard or how fast we ran. Scripture doesn't pretend we can out-hustle that one. No amount of sleepless striving frees a soul that's bankrupt before God.

But here is where the gospel quietly answers the very language this proverb uses. The Bible actually borrows the word for what the son in Proverbs 6 became — a guarantor, someone who stands legally good for another's debt — and applies it to Jesus. “Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22, NIV). Where the neighbor in Proverbs 6 was a guarantor who might fail — who might not have the money when the bill came due, who might vanish, who might himself need rescuing — Jesus is a guarantor who cannot default. He “always lives” to make good on what he promised (Hebrews 7:24-25). He didn't co-sign our debt from a safe distance. He paid it outright, in full, with his own life.

So the practical wisdom of Proverbs 6 still stands, and it's worth taking seriously this week if there's a promise, a pledge, or a commitment sitting heavy on your chest right now. Don't let embarrassment talk you into waiting. If there's a conversation you've been putting off, a debt you need to address, a word you gave that's now costing you sleep, wisdom says: go today, go humbly, go while you still can, and don't rest until it's resolved. That kind of urgency isn't anxiety. It's respect for how real entanglement actually works.

But underneath that urgency, rest in this: the debt that could have held you forever has already been paid by a Guarantor who never fails and never disappears. You don't have to thrash alone in that snare. Somebody already went in, at the point of exhaustion, and did not stop until you were free.
